order_a_first.reason: A is substantially closer to the hidden target because it proposes elemental-powder mechanical alloying followed by SPS, nanocrystalline refinement, and an FCC/BCC-type phase constitution with grain-boundary and solid-solution strengthening. It nevertheless misses the CoCrFeNiTi composition, short 1–6 h milling window, exact SPS conditions, phase fractions, and target properties; its FCC phase is also described as TiO rather than a second solid solution, and its falsification test does not cleanly separate Hall–Petch strengthening from solid-solution strengthening. B departs more fundamentally by proposing rapid solidification plus sub-solvus annealing and BCC+B2 ordering in refractory alloys. Its claimed VEC window is contradicted by its own evidence, which associates VEC ≤4.4 with ductility and ≥4.6 with brittleness, and ordered B2 is inconsistent with the requested avoidance of brittle intermetallic formation.

order_b_first.reason: B is closer to the hidden target because it proposes elemental-powder mechanical alloying followed by SPS under inert/controlled conditions, with nanocrystalline refinement, a dual BCC/FCC constitution, and grain-boundary plus solid-solution strengthening. A instead substitutes rapid solidification/sub-solvus annealing and a BCC+B2 refractory-alloy mechanism, far from the target CoCrFeNiTi HEBM–SPS route and FCC/BCC phase mixture. B nevertheless misses key target details: it uses NbMoTaWVTi, 40 h milling and higher SPS temperatures rather than CoCrFeNiTi, 1–6 h and 900–1000 °C; treats TiO contamination as the FCC phase despite claiming oxidation avoidance and no brittle secondary compounds; predicts unsupported properties; and its falsification test probes thermal stability rather than distinguishing Hall–Petch/dislocation strengthening from simple solid-solution strengthening.
